title: Congo's Ebola Outbreak Becomes Deadliest Ever, Topping 4,000 Deaths
summary:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo is battling the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Health officials said Thursday that 4,018 people have died out of 8,300 confirmed cases — nearly half. The outbreak was declared on May 15 and is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved treatment or vaccine.

The crisis is centered in Ituri province in northeastern Congo. Front-line health workers, including teams that track people exposed to patients, have gone on strike several times because they haven't been paid for months. This week, they protested in Bunia, the provincial capital, holding signs reading "No money, no data!" before officials dispersed them.

Violence is making things worse. A senior UN official, Julien Harneis, said soldiers burned an Ebola transit camp near Bunia while searching for weapons. About 19,000 people in the camp had to flee. "When we lose a centre, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment and we have to start again," Harneis said. "And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need."

More than 50 health workers have died from the virus. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) was infected and flown to the Netherlands for treatment in a high-level isolation unit.

There are mixed signals about the outbreak's path. New confirmed cases have dropped from about 850 a week in mid-July to around 490 in September, according to Africa CDC. However, experts warn this drop may be partly due to insecurity and difficulty getting communities to cooperate — not because the virus is truly under control. The World Health Organization has also warned the virus is spreading into new areas.

A Congolese politician was beaten to death this week for defending the government's response, showing how tense the situation has become.
why_it_matters: Outbreaks in conflict zones are everyone's problem: when surveillance, pay and access break down, a virus can spread into new regions before it is understood, and this strain has no approved vaccine or treatment — a gap in global health that affects how fast the next epidemic can be stopped.

background_read: Ebola is a severe viral disease first identified in 1976 near the Ebola River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), a large country in central Africa. Since then the DRC has faced many outbreaks, including a 2018–2020 outbreak in North Kivu that was the second-largest ever recorded and was finally contained with an experimental vaccine.

The Bundibugyo species of the virus was first identified in Uganda in 2007. The vaccines and antibody treatments that now exist are approved for the Zaire species, not for Bundibugyo, which is why this outbreak is so hard to fight. The World Health Organization (WHO) is the United Nations agency that coordinates responses to global health emergencies, and Africa CDC is the public health agency of the African Union. Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) is an international medical charity that sends teams into conflict zones.

Ituri province, in northeastern DRC, has suffered decades of armed conflict and is a major gold-mining area, so armed groups, displaced people and weak roads all make tracking and treating the virus extremely difficult.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — health officials and aid agencies
perspectives.description: Africa CDC reports that weekly confirmed cases have fallen sharply, from about 850 in mid-July to around 490 in September, and international groups such as MSF were able to evacuate and treat an infected staff member in a high-level isolation unit abroad — evidence that global response systems still function.

Front-line teams and contact tracers say they have not been paid for months while more than 50 health workers have died, so they protest with signs reading 'No money, no data!' They argue that the people most at risk are being asked to carry the response without pay or protection.

Case numbers collected in a conflict zone are unreliable. The fall in reported cases may reflect insecurity, burned transit camps and communities refusing to cooperate rather than genuine control, and without a Bundibugyo vaccine, isolation and contact tracing are the only real tools.

The outbreak shows the need to develop vaccines and treatments for Ebola species beyond Zaire, to negotiate safe access with armed groups, and to pay health workers on time so that response teams do not walk off the job in the middle of an epidemic.
